content: Bronchopneumonia was first recognized by Hippocrates and later described in detail by Laennec in 1819. In 1842, Rokitansky differentiated pneumonia into two types: bronchopneumonia and lobar pneumonia. Pneumonia can be classified based on the anatomical distribution of lung consolidation into two subtypes: lobar pneumonia and lobular pneumonia (bronchopneumonia). The pathophysiology of bronchopneumonia involves inflammation of the lung parenchyma. On gross pathology, it is characterized by multiple foci of consolidation, which are typically bilateral and most commonly found in the basal lobes. These lesions are 2–4 cm in diameter, gray-yellow in color, dry, poorly demarcated, and often centered around a bronchus. They tend to coalesce, especially in children. Microscopically, bronchopneumonia shows inflammatory condensation centered around a bronchiole with acute bronchiolitis. The alveolar lumens surrounding the bronchi are filled with neutrophils and suppurative exudate, a condition referred to as leukocytic alveolitis. There is also significant congestion, and the inflammatory foci are separated by normal, aerated lung parenchyma. Bronchopneumonia is most commonly caused by pneumococcal serotypes 3, 7, 8, 10, 18, and 20. Common mechanisms of pneumonia development include micro-aspiration, hematogenous spread, spread from a contiguous focus, and macro-aspiration. It is often associated with infections caused by gram-negative bacteria, Staphylococcus aureus, and certain fungi. The clinical features of bronchopneumonia include cough, fever, chills, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and sputum production. However, these symptoms may be absent in older patients. Gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea can also occur. Older patients may present with altered mental status. Bronchopneumonia must be differentiated from other diseases that cause similar clinical symptoms and interstitial infiltrates on chest X-rays, such as lobar pneumonia, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, collagen vascular disease, asbestosis, drug toxicities, pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary edema, pulmonary embolism, neoplastic lesions, and other types of pneumonia like cryptogenic pneumonia. Bronchopneumonia can affect patients of all age groups but is more commonly observed in elderly individuals. It is also more prevalent in men than women and is more frequently seen in Black individuals compared to Caucasians. Risk factors for developing bronchopneumonia include influenza infection, alcohol abuse, hyposplenism or splenectomy, smoking, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), asthma, and immunocompromised states. Additional risk factors include homelessness, incarceration, pregnancy, crack cocaine use, opioid use, and occupational exposure such as welding. Risk factors for a complicated course include older age, preexisting lung conditions, immunodeficiency or AIDS, and nosocomial infections. The natural history of bronchopneumonia begins with early symptoms such as sudden fever, chills, cough, and chest pain. If untreated, the condition may progress to tachypnea and increasing systemic toxicity, potentially leading to lobar pneumonia. Common complications include parapneumonic effusion, empyema, necrotizing pneumonia, lung abscess, and metastatic infections such as endocarditis, septic arthritis, peritonitis, pericarditis, and meningitis. Cardiac complications may also occur. The diagnosis of bronchopneumonia is based on clinical and radiological evidence. Symptoms include fever, chills, cough, chest pain, and shortness of breath. Physical examination findings may include fever, tachypnea (respiratory rate >24 breaths/min), tachycardia, and chest examination findings such as audible crackles, decreased or bronchial breath sounds, dullness to percussion in areas of consolidation, tactile fremitus, and egophony. There are no specific laboratory findings for bronchopneumonia. Leukocytosis (15,000–30,000 per mm³) with a leftward shift on blood tests can aid in diagnosis. Elevated ESR or CRP levels indicate nonspecific inflammation. Chest X-ray is the imaging modality of choice for bronchopneumonia. It typically shows peribronchial thickening and poorly defined air-space opacities. Inhomogeneous patchy areas of consolidation involving several lobes indicate more severe disease. When confluent, bronchopneumonia may resemble lobar pneumonia. If the chest X-ray is negative but clinical suspicion is high, HRCT can confirm the diagnosis due to its higher sensitivity and accuracy in detecting lesions and anatomical changes. In emergencies where chest X-ray and HRCT are unavailable, lung ultrasound performed by an experienced physician can provide diagnostic findings. Microbial analysis in bronchopneumonia can be performed using blood cultures, sputum analysis, PCR, and urine antigen detection. However, pathogens are not commonly identified, and empiric treatment should be initiated once the diagnosis is made. The primary treatment for bronchopneumonia involves antibiotics and supportive care. The choice of antibiotics depends on the epidemiology of microbes, resistance patterns, patient comorbidities, and illness severity. In patients without comorbidities, macrolides such as azithromycin and clarithromycin are effective. For macrolide-resistant pneumonias or patients with multiple comorbidities, doxycycline, amoxicillin-clavulanate, and cephalosporins like cefpodoxime and cefuroxime may be used. Response to antibiotics can be monitored through clinical improvement, serum inflammatory markers, and chest X-ray findings. Most uncomplicated pneumonias are treated on an outpatient basis, requiring only two follow-up visits to assess clinical improvement and resolution. Follow-up chest X-rays are recommended only for male patients over 50 years of age and smokers. Prevention of bronchopneumonia includes vaccination against influenza and pneumococcal antigens, as well as smoking cessation. Pneumococcal vaccination is particularly indicated for patients over the age of 65.
